newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico union leader predicts labor split.
newsitem.headline: Mexico union leader predicts labor split.

text.p: Shaken by growing dissent in its ranks, Mexico's official labour movement faces its biggest threat in decades as increasing numbers of unions plot to defect from the pro-government Labour Congress (CT), a dissident union leader said Thursday.

Some 25 labour unions plan to meet on July 31 and vote on whether to split from the CT and its legendary nonagenarian leader Fidel Velazquez, who since 1928 has kept Mexican labour firmly under the thumb of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

The dissident unions, which include the Telephone Workers' Union, the Electricity Workers' Union, the Automotive Industry Union and the Social Security (IMSS) Union, together claim 3 million members. The CT, which claims 10 million in its ranks, says the dissident unions' members amount to only half a million workers.

Francisco Hernandez Juarez, leader of the influential Telephone Workers' Union, knows his union will vote for independence and hopes many of the others will do the same -- ending the CT's iron grip on the Mexican worker.
"We know we want to leave, but we don't want to do it alone. If just the telephone workers were independent, it would open us up to all sorts of aggression," Hernandez Juarez said in an interview.
Real wages in Mexico have fallen sharply during the past two decades through a series of economic crises but labour unrest here has been virtually non-existant.
When the peso crashed more than two years ago, inflation again skyrocketed and real wages fell sharply. This year, economists predict real wages will likely remain flat.
"Unionism is supposed to be accommodating enough to represent all workers and defend their interests despite their political colour," Hernandez Juarez said.
But, he added, the CT "has shown clearly that it is incapable of defending the Mexican worker."

Signs of trouble in the official labour movement surfaced last year, when a handful of unions belonging to the CT marched during the May Day parade despite an official ban on marches due to fear of unrest.
Recently, Velazquez has lashed out at Hernandez Juarez due to the threat of a split in the CT's ranks, calling the union leader a "homosexual."
Hernandez Juarez said the 96-year-old Velazquez is striking out because he did not think that the 25 unions would agree on a congress to discuss splitting the CT.

Velazquez recently said workers would be allowed to march during this year's May Day parade, a move Hernandez Juarez said was aimed at trying to convince workers their situation was improving ahead of key mid-term elections in early July.
